rationale: actions/checkout writes the runner's ephemeral GITHUB_TOKEN into .git/config. Without this the whole-tree scan fails on every CI run on a token the platform injected itself -- a guaranteed false positive, not a finding.
Cargo build output. Contains compiled copies of source strings, so scanning it re-reports whatever the source already had, at enormous cost.
Vendored JS dependencies. Their docs and fixtures legitimately contain example credentials (URI-style user:pass@ hosts); none are this project's secrets.
Yarn's zero-install cache for crates/command-signatures-v2/js. Same reasoning as node_modules.
A dependency lockfile: names, versions and checksums. No credentials, and it is large enough to slow every scan.
Same as Cargo.lock, for the JS sub-package.
Same as Cargo.lock, for the JS sub-package.
Recorded gate baselines: literal lists of strings found in the tree. A scanner walking them re-reports whatever they record, so a finding here is always a duplicate of a finding elsewhere.
Same as the baselines -- these files exist to record what the gates found.

Upstream's fixtures for the product's own secret-REDACTION feature. The file states the keys are fake, and their hashes differ from any real credential. The tests exist precisely to stop real secrets reaching logs; deleting the fixtures to quiet the scanner would remove that protection.
Binary sqlite fixtures for the integration suite; the URI-style user:pass@host strings are serialised sample rows, not credentials.
Fake Stripe/GitHub keys that are the INPUT to the product's own secret-redaction tests. Removing them to quiet the scanner would delete the protection they verify.
URI literals exercising git credential-handling paths.
URI literals exercising websocket proxy URL parsing.
A URI literal in terminal input parsing tests.
A URI literal used by semantic-selection tests.
Packaged release artifacts: copies of the built binary, so findings duplicate the source. 290 MB per scan with brotli decode errors on compressed Mach-O sections.

HarnessAvailabilityEvent lost its `Changed` variant when the harness catalog became a static local list, leaving only auth-secret events, which all share an `AuthSecret` prefix. The prefix is accurate, not lazy naming: every remaining variant really is about one subsystem. Renaming them to satisfy the lint would make them less descriptive across five subscriber files, and the alternative -- keeping a `Changed` variant nothing can ever emit -- is worse. Revisit when the cloud auth-secret subsystem is removed and this enum goes with it.
